name: Battery recycling and materials recovery
summary: Recycling plants recover usable lithium, nickel, cobalt and other materials from battery manufacturing scrap and retired batteries.
useCase: A battery manufacturer sends off-spec cells and scrap to a nearby recycler, then buys recovered material that meets its production specifications.
whyNow: The IEA reported that lithium-ion battery recycling capacity expanded by 50% in 2023. Near-term feedstock is often factory scrap; the large wave of retired EV batteries arrives later and varies with vehicle life and second-use decisions. More capacity is not automatically better economics: the IEA found that announced 2030 recycling capacity could substantially exceed available feedstock. Metal prices, chemistry shifts toward lower-value LFP, collection logistics and material qualification determine margins. Current 2026 funding announcements from Altilium and cylib show continued development, while sector restructuring is a reminder to track plants with secured input and customers rather than announced capacity alone.

mainstream.scope: Routine closed-loop procurement and recycling of battery production scrap and growing EV-retirement streams in major battery-manufacturing regions.
mainstream.rationale: Industrial recycling already exists, particularly in China. The emerging phase is efficient lithium recovery, wider LFP processing and dependable regional closed loops. Rising collected volumes and qualification with cell makers could make these routine around the end of the decade. Low metal prices or underutilised plants can cause consolidation and delay regional expansion.

metric.name: Global lithium-ion battery recycling capacity index
metric.scope: Index derived only from IEA’s reported 50% increase in recycling capacity during 2023.
metric.limitations: The index preserves the published growth rate without inventing absolute tonnage. Capacity is not throughput, recovered output, revenue or utilisation. No comparable annual 2024–2026 global throughput series was established.
metric.futureNote: No defensible comparable external deployment forecast found. The separate maturity path is an analyst scenario, not measured adoption.

milestones.text: The selected sources do not provide a comparable annual global throughput measurement; existing industrial recycling predates this assessment.
Reference year for the index; 100 is a normalisation, not a claim of 100 plants or tonnes.
IEA reported a 50% increase in lithium-ion battery recycling capacity.
IEA’s recycling review highlighted policy momentum and a possible mismatch between announced capacity and available battery scrap.
cylib announced support for expanding European recycling, illustrating continued regional investment rather than measured global throughput.
Altilium announced follow-on investment from SQM and Marubeni on 6 October to support battery-materials scale-up; this is financing, not commissioned output.

tailwinds: Manufacturing scrap provides relatively concentrated, known-chemistry feedstock.
Supply-chain resilience and customer sourcing requirements support recovered materials.
Improved process recovery and reuse of material can reduce dependence on newly mined inputs.
bottlenecks: Plants can be built before enough batteries reach end of life.
LFP contains less high-value nickel and cobalt, challenging some business models.
Collection, safe transport, impurity control and customer qualification add cost.
watchMetrics: Actual tonnes processed, utilisation and recovered battery-grade lithium output.
Secured feedstock and offtake relative to installed capacity; avoid adding mutually exclusive announcements.
Recovery yield, energy/water use and net margin by battery chemistry at current metal prices.
